title: Genesis 8. The Cup Recedes.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 8. The Cup Recedes.
God remembered Noah.
Not that He forgot.
The memory of God is not the recovery of information,
it is movement toward.
God remembers, and the remembering becomes action.
He remembers Noah, every animal,
every creature that was with him in the ark.
And God made a wind pass over the earth.
The word is ruach, wind, breath, Spirit.
The same Hebrew word appeared over the waters in chapter one.
Here God causes a ruach to pass over the earth,
and the waters begin to recede.
Same word.
Different scene.
Creation and re-creation.
The Cup that was poured out begins to recede.
The fountains of the deep are closed.
The windows of heaven are shut.
The rain is restrained.
What God opened, He closes.
The boundaries that were undone in chapter seven are being redrawn,
not all at once, but steadily.
The waters retreat.
They go and return, go and return, a long, slow withdrawal.
The ark comes to rest.
In the seventh month, on the seventeenth day,
it rests on the mountains of Ararat.
The vessel that has been floating for five months touches ground.
It does not land on a plain.
It lands on a mountain.
The waters have descended far enough that the highest peaks break the surface,
the same peaks that were covered by fifteen cubits in the previous chapter are now visible.
The waters keep receding.
By the tenth month, the tops of the mountains appear.
Noah waits forty days.
Then he opens the window of the ark, the window he made,
and sends out a raven.
The raven goes.
It flies back and forth.
It never comes back inside.
It finds nothing to rest on,
but it does not return to the ark.
It keeps going out and coming back, out and back,
waiting for the water to dry.
The raven is a creature of endurance, not of finding.
It circles what is not yet ready.
Then Noah sends a dove.
The dove goes out to see if the waters have subsided.
She finds no place to rest her foot.
Water is still on the face of the whole earth.
She returns to him, to the ark.
He puts out his hand, takes her and brings her in.
Noah reaches for the dove the way God reached for him,
drawing life back into the vessel.
He waits seven more days.
He sends the dove again.
She comes back at evening.
In her mouth, a freshly plucked olive leaf.
The first sign that what was buried has begun to grow.
Life is returning to the earth that was drowned.
The leaf is not a promise.
It is a witness.
The Cup is receding,
and what it leaves behind is not only mud and death.
Something is growing.
He waits seven more days.
He sends the dove.
She does not return.
The dove has found a home.
What was inside the ark has stepped outside and stayed.
The creature that could not find rest now rests.
The vessel that held life through death has released its first inhabitant into a world that can receive her.
In the six hundred and first year, the first month,
the first day, the waters are dried from the earth.
Noah removes the covering of the ark and looks.
The surface of the ground is dry.
By the second month, the twenty-seventh day, the earth is dry.
Then God speaks: Go out of the ark.
You, your wife, your sons, your sons' wives.
Bring out every living thing that is with you, birds, livestock,
every creeping thing.
Let them breed abundantly on the earth.
Be fruitful.
Multiply.
The command given in chapter one, be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth,
is spoken again.
The same words.
The same blessing.
To a world that has been emptied.
To creatures that have been held inside a vessel for over a year.
The rhythm of creation is spoken into what looks like a world that has died.
What God said at the beginning, He says again after the end.
Noah goes out.
His sons, his wife, his sons' wives.
Every animal, every creeping thing, every bird, after their families,
they go out of the ark.
The door that God shut in chapter seven is now open.
What was held inside the Cup of judgment is released.
The creatures that came in two by two now walk out into a world that has no other living thing in it.
And the first thing Noah does is build an altar.
Not commanded.
Not instructed.
Not described as a response to a voice.
He builds it.
The first altar in Scripture.
He takes from every clean animal and every clean bird and offers burnt offerings on it.
The Cup that was poured out in judgment is now answered with a cup of offering.
Worship rises from a man who survived what should have killed him.
The creature that was preserved in the ark offers back to the God who preserved him,
from the very animals God brought to him.
The Lord smelled the pleasing aroma.
And the Lord said in His heart:
I will never again curse the ground because of man.
For the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth.
Neither will I ever again strike every living thing as I have done.
God does not say man has changed.
He says the opposite,
the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth.
What He judged in chapter six, He still sees.
The difference is not in man.
The difference is in God's own heart.
He chooses restraint.
The Cup that was poured out will not be poured out this way again,
not because the evil is gone, but because God says so.
Inside Himself.
To Himself.
While the earth remains, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat,
summer and winter, day and night shall not cease.
The rhythm returns.
The seasons that were drowned come back.
The evening and morning that structured creation in chapter one,
that were disrupted by forty days of rain and a hundred and fifty days of flood,
are re-established.
Time restarts.
The Cup recedes, and what is left behind is not paradise.
It is the possibility of beginning again, under the same sky,
on the same ground, with the same heart,
held by a promise that lives inside God's own chest.
